::: {.oneline}
An exciton appears as a resonance below the energy needed to free an electron,
since the electron and the hole it leaves behind attract each other and remain
bound.
:::

## Short answer

Absorbing light does not add or remove an electron, but moves one, leaving an
empty state behind. What the sample then contains is a pair, that is, a
negatively charged electron somewhere it was not, and a positively charged hole
where it used to be. The two attract.

This attraction means that the pair can be created with less energy than would
be needed to separate the two completely. Absorption therefore begins *below*
the gap, at discrete energies corresponding to bound states of the pair, in a
series reminiscent of a hydrogen atom, though with the Coulomb attraction
weakened by the screening of all the other electrons and with the motion of the
pair governed by the band structure rather than by free space.

This is why an exciton cannot appear in a band structure. A band structure
answers the question of what it costs to add or remove one electron, whereas an
exciton is neutral, since nothing was added or removed. It lives in the response
function, which is precisely the object describing what happens when the system
is disturbed without changing its charge.

Two competing effects also explain a recurring surprise. Interactions push the
gap up, while the electron–hole attraction pulls the absorption onset back down.
In two-dimensional materials both are large and they cancel substantially, so
that a calculation including neither can look deceptively reasonable for
entirely wrong reasons.

## Why it works this way

Whether excitons matter is a question of screening. In a good metal the
attraction is screened away so effectively that no bound state survives. In a
monolayer semiconductor the field lines leave the material and are barely
screened at all, so that binding energies reach hundreds of millielectronvolts
and excitons dominate the optical response at room temperature.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The algebra: the Bethe–Salpeter equation

The electron–hole pair satisfies an eigenvalue problem in the space of
transitions from occupied state $v$ to empty state $c$ at wavevector
$\mathbf k$:

$$
(\varepsilon_{c\mathbf k} - \varepsilon_{v\mathbf k}) A^{S}_{vc\mathbf k}
+ \sum_{v'c'\mathbf k'} K_{vc\mathbf k,\, v'c'\mathbf k'}\,
A^{S}_{v'c'\mathbf k'}
= E^{S} A^{S}_{vc\mathbf k} ,
$$ {#eq-bse}

where the single-particle energies come from a quasiparticle calculation and the
kernel $K$ contains an attractive screened direct term together with a repulsive
exchange term. The eigenvalues $E^{S}$ are the excitation energies, while the
eigenvectors give the oscillator strengths and therefore determine which
excitons are bright and which are dark.
:::

## Common confusions

- **"The exciton binding energy is the gap minus the peak position."** Only if
  the gap is the quasiparticle gap, and not the one obtained from a
  ground-state calculation.
- **"Dark excitons do not exist."** They exist, and simply do not couple to
  light at leading order, though they often dominate what happens after
  absorption.
- **"An exciton is a small hydrogen atom."** The analogy fails once the binding
  is strong enough that the pair fits within a few unit cells.
